title: Suppressing Self-Discharging of Quantum Batteries by Cavity Interactions
authors: Anass Jad, Abderrahim El Allati, Mohammad B. Arjmandi
abstract: We analyse a two-cavity architecture, in which a lossy cavity hosting $N$ qubits is coherently coupled to an auxiliary cavity, as a resource for the storage phase of an open quantum battery at non-zero temperature. Within a local Lindblad treatment in the resonant configuration, we find that the inter-cavity coupling enhances the suppression of self-discharging across every initial preparation, battery size, and temperature we examine, with the protection degrading smoothly as the mean thermal occupation increases. For a single qubit, the energy-basis coherence of a pure superposition leads to better long-time retention than fully excited state, highlighting the beneficial role of quantum coherence in protecting stored energy against thermal degradation. For two-qubit batteries, Bell-state preparations exhibit enhanced long-time ergotropy retention compared with the fully excited state, while the inclusion of qubit-qubit interactions produces only a weak dependence on the interaction type and strength within the parameter regime considered. Extending the analysis to multi-qubit GHZ-charged batteries with all-to-all Heisenberg interactions, we find that the normalized retained ergotropy increases monotonically with the number of qubits. This behavior is consistent with the collective enhancement of the qubit-cavity coupling in the symmetric Dicke manifold, indicating that larger quantum batteries can benefit from improved protection against self-discharge. These findings establish cavity-assisted protection as a promising strategy for mitigating self-discharging and realizing of long-lived quantum batteries in experimentally accessible platforms.
summary: The paper investigates how coupling a quantum battery's primary cavity to an auxiliary cavity can suppress energy loss mechanisms causing self-discharge. By analyzing ergotropy retention across single, two-, and multi-qubit systems, the authors show that inter-cavity coupling is highly beneficial. This establishes cavity-assisted protection as a robust strategy for building long-lived quantum energy storage devices.
main_problem: The primary goal is suppressing the self-discharging of stored quantum work (ergotropy) in a quantum battery due to energy leakage into the environment.
main_result: Inter-cavity coupling significantly enhances the protection against self-discharge, and for multi-qubit systems, the retained ergotropy increases monotonically with the number of qubits due to collective effects.
method: The analysis uses a local Lindblad master equation treatment applied to a two-cavity architecture coupled to $N$ qubits.
model_or_system: The system consists of $N$ qubits in a lossy cavity ($C1$), which is coherently coupled to an auxiliary cavity ($C2$). The dynamics are governed by the full Hamiltonian and dissipation channels, analyzed under resonant conditions.
key_observables: Ergotropy, $W(ho_B)$, defined as the maximum extractable work unitarily from the reduced battery state $ho_B$.
important_parameters: Inter-cavity coupling strength ($J$), qubit-cavity coupling ($\kappa$), and mean thermal occupation ($ ar{n}$) characterizing finite temperature.
main_assumptions: The analysis employs a local Lindblad treatment, assuming the system is in the weak-coupling Markovian regime.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how retained ergotropy ($W(t)/W(0)$) depends on $J/\Gamma_1$ (showing enhancement with coupling), and demonstrate size scaling for GHZ states, showing increasing retention with $N$.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the problem starting from single-qubit systems, progressing to two-qubit entangled states (Bell states), and culminating in multi-qubit GHZ-charged batteries to establish scaling laws.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses energy storage limitations in quantum devices by engineering structured environments (the auxiliary cavity) to protect stored coherence and extractable work, a key topic in open quantum systems and quantum thermodynamics.

A collection of N identical qubits {q1, q2, . . . , qN} of transition fre- quency ω0 is embedded in a common lossy cavity C1 (frequency ω1, decay rate Γ1) with which each qubit interacts at the same coupling strength κ. The cavity C1 is coherently coupled to an auxiliary cavity C2 (frequency ω2, decay rate Γ2) through a photon-exchange cou- pling of strength J.
